title: Alternatives to 12-Step Programs
involves: Read about recovery groups other than 12-step programs, such as SMART Recovery, Women for Sobriety, and secular or faith-based groups, then jot down a meeting to try.
benefits: Shows that there are many paths to peer support, so a person can find a group whose approach fits them.

title: Introduction to 12-Step Programs
involves: Read a short overview of 12-step programs such as AA: how they began, the main types of meetings, their spiritual but not religious side, and how to find a meeting.
benefits: Helps a person decide whether peer support meetings might fit them and makes trying a first meeting feel less daunting.

title: Introduction to Sponsors
involves: Read about what a 12-step sponsor is, what sponsors do, and how to choose one.
benefits: Explains how a sponsor can offer guidance, accountability, and support during hard moments, and what to look for before asking someone.

title: Refusal Skills Practice
involves: Fill out a worksheet that pictures a realistic moment when a drink is offered, write two or three ways to say no plus a backup line, and plan what to do right after.
benefits: Rehearsing refusals ahead of time builds confidence and makes it easier to say no when there is pressure to drink.

title: Noticing Alcohol Scripts
involves: Fill out a worksheet about a risky setting: when and with whom a person goes there, the automatic thoughts about drinking that come up, and how strong the urge feels.
benefits: Spotting automatic drinking thoughts creates a pause between the thought and the action, which is the first step toward changing it.

title: Rewriting Alcohol Scripts
involves: Take one automatic thought about drinking, check the evidence for and against it, weigh its short- and long-term effects, write a more helpful replacement, and rehearse using it.
benefits: Replacing an unhelpful thought with a realistic one changes how a person feels and acts in situations where drinking used to be automatic.

title: Managing Anger
involves: Answer a few questions about how anger shows up in the body and in behavior, then choose from a list of healthy ways to cope with it.
benefits: Anger can build quickly and lead toward drinking; recognizing it early and having other outlets ready keeps it from taking over.

title: Assertiveness in Recovery
involves: Learn the difference between assertive, passive, and aggressive responses, then write and practice three short boundary statements and a reply for when someone pushes back.
benefits: Having calm, clear words ready makes it easier to protect recovery when offered a drink or pressured to stay somewhere risky.

title: Noticing Physical Sensations
involves: Spend 5 to 10 minutes slowly moving attention from the feet to the head and noticing sensations without judging them, with a guided recording if desired.
benefits: Urges, stress, and emotions often show up in the body first, so noticing them early leaves more time to use a coping skill.

title: Understanding Boredom in Recovery
involves: Read why life can feel boring after stopping drinking, list five activities to try, and reflect on old and new interests.
benefits: Boredom is common early in recovery and fades with time; planning engaging activities fills the gap in the meantime.

title: Compassionate U-Turn
involves: Learn a four-step script (notice, normalize, refocus, reconnect) to use when feeling off track, discouraged, or self-critical.
benefits: Gives a quick, kind way to reset when things feel off track, so a hard moment is less likely to spiral.

title: Self-Help Groups
involves: Read short descriptions of five self-help groups (AA, SMART Recovery, Refuge Recovery, LifeRing, and Women for Sobriety), visit their websites, and consider a next step.
benefits: Comparing groups helps a person find support that fits their beliefs and style; the benefits of meetings grow with repeated visits.

title: Urges Log
involves: Keep a log through the day of each urge to drink: the situation, how strong it was, and what was done to cope.
benefits: Tracking urges shows patterns in what sets them off and which coping steps work best.

title: Craving Plan
involves: Read about four ways to cope with urges (distraction, talking it through, urge surfing, and challenging thoughts) and choose two or three to plan out in advance.
benefits: Having a plan ready before an urge shows up makes it easier to ride it out without drinking.

title: Craving Triggers
involves: Read about the people, places, feelings, and physical states that commonly set off urges, list personal triggers, and circle the ones that can be avoided.
benefits: Knowing what sets off urges makes it possible to cut down exposure to them and to be ready for the ones that cannot be avoided.

title: Learning From the Day
involves: Answer five short questions about the day: one recovery action taken, a challenge that came up, how it was handled, what was learned, and one change for tomorrow.
benefits: Turns everyday experience into useful feedback and helps catch small problems before they grow into bigger setbacks.

title: Pros and Cons of Alcohol Use vs. Recovery
involves: Fill in a simple grid listing the short- and long-term benefits and costs of recovery and of drinking.
benefits: Laying out both sides helps a person base choices on the full picture rather than a passing urge, and gives them something to reread when bargaining thoughts come up.

title: Coping With Depression in Recovery
involves: Check off recent signs of low mood, note how they affect daily life and recovery, choose two or three coping actions, and decide when to reach out for help.
benefits: Low mood can raise the risk of drinking; spotting early signs and having a plan ready allows a response before it deepens.

title: Personal Emergency Plan
involves: Review a five-step plan for moments when the pull to drink is strong (leave, wait 15 minutes, challenge the thought, refocus, recall past successes) and fill in a list of people to call.
benefits: Having steps and contacts ready ahead of time makes it easier to ride out a strong urge without drinking.

title: Understanding Emotional Avoidance
involves: Pick a place that is avoided because of the feelings it brings up, rate those feelings, and weigh the short-term benefits and long-term costs of avoiding it.
benefits: Helps a person see whether avoiding a place is protecting recovery or holding them back, so avoidance becomes a choice rather than a habit.

title: Choosing Your Next Step
involves: Rate readiness to face a place that has been avoided, then choose either to keep skipping it for now or to plan one small, supported step back toward it, with a way to leave if needed.
benefits: Supports paced, intentional choices about difficult places, so a person neither pushes too soon nor avoids by default.

title: Emotional Buildup
involves: Read how stress and difficult feelings pile up when ignored, rate today's pressure level, name what is driving it, and pick one small release action.
benefits: Small, regular releases keep emotional pressure from building to the point where urges or conflict spike.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Emotional Places
involves: Answer five questions about places that stir up mixed feelings, the small decisions that lead there, warning signs, and ways to take care of oneself before, during, and after a visit.
benefits: Noticing the chain of choices early makes it easier to stop before ending up in an emotionally risky situation.

title: Emotional Triggers
involves: Read about three feelings often tied to drinking (loneliness, anger, and feeling deprived) and reflect on which have been triggers in the past.
benefits: Treating these feelings as red flags, rather than trying to avoid them, lets a person respond before they lead toward drinking.

title: Understanding Emotions
involves: Find a quiet place and spend a few minutes writing freely in answer to a question about current feelings, without worrying about spelling or style.
benefits: Putting feelings into words makes them clearer and helps prevent the emotional buildup that can lead to relapse.

title: Understanding Your Feelings
involves: Reflect on recent emotions, how they show up in the body, and usual reactions, and practice naming feelings more precisely than 'a bad day.'
benefits: Naming emotions accurately makes it easier to choose a helpful response and lowers the risk of acting on impulse.

title: Exit Plan
involves: Build a personal 1-10 warning scale, set the level at which to leave, choose a quick exit routine and one simple phrase to say, and mentally rehearse leaving.
benefits: Deciding in advance removes the need to think things through in a high-risk moment, so leaving becomes quick and automatic.

title: Finances and Recovery
involves: Read how both money stress and extra cash can lead toward drinking, then reflect on personal money triggers and one small, healthy step to take when they come up.
benefits: Noticing money-related triggers early helps a person respond with problem-solving instead of escape.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Time with Friends
involves: Answer five questions about friends or social settings that raise urges, the small decisions that lead into them, warning signs, and boundaries or plans that help.
benefits: Helps a person stay socially connected while catching risky social choices early, when they are easiest to change.

title: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Exercise
involves: Notice five things to see, four to touch, three sounds, two smells, and one taste in the immediate surroundings; it takes a few minutes and can be done anywhere.
benefits: Bringing attention to the present calms the mind and body, and regular practice makes the skill easier to use during stress.

title: HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired
involves: A two-minute check-in: rate hunger, anger, loneliness, and tiredness from 0 to 10, pick a quick action for any that are high, then rate them again.
benefits: Catches everyday states that wear down coping, so they can be eased before urges build.

title: Illness
involves: Read why getting sick can raise relapse risk (breaks in routine, time alone, using sickness as an excuse) and healthy habits that help prevent illness and speed recovery from it.
benefits: Knowing that illness is a risky time helps a person protect their recovery routine when they feel unwell.

title: Internal Triggers
involves: Through the day, record strong feelings or urges noticed inside, how intense they were, what was done instead of drinking, and how things felt 20 minutes later.
benefits: Noticing and naming inner triggers creates space between a feeling and acting on it, which builds the habit of responding on purpose.

title: Seemingly Irrelevant Decisions
involves: Read about small, harmless-seeming choices (like taking a route home past a familiar bar) that gradually lead toward drinking, and the red-flag thoughts that often come with them.
benefits: Learning to spot these choices early makes it possible to change course before risk builds.

title: Exploring Justifications for Drinking: Celebrating
involves: Check off common thoughts that make drinking seem OK during celebrations, vacations, or good times, and plan how to respond when they come up.
benefits: Recognizing these thoughts ahead of time makes it easier to question them before they lead to drinking.

title: Exploring Justifications for Drinking: Negative Emotions
involves: Check off common thoughts that make drinking seem like the answer when feeling down, angry, lonely, or afraid, and name who to reach out to when they come up.
benefits: Questioning these thoughts, and having support ready, makes it easier to get through hard feelings without drinking.

title: Justifications for Drinking
involves: Read how justifications for drinking make it seem reasonable, how they can lead step by step back to drinking, early warning signs, and ways to challenge them.
benefits: Knowing that a return to drinking often starts with thinking helps a person catch these thoughts early.

title: Exploring Justifications for Drinking: Testing
involves: Check off common thoughts about proving strength by being around alcohol or old drinking friends, and plan a response for when these thoughts come up.
benefits: Reinforces that being smart, not strong, protects recovery, and makes it easier to pass on situations that put willpower to the test.

title: Making New Friends in Recovery
involves: List the people most time is spent with and whether they support recovery, check off what feels missing and what makes new friendships hard, and complete two sentence prompts.
benefits: Building supportive friendships through shared activities reduces isolation and is one of the strongest supports for recovery.

title: Making New Friends
involves: Answer six questions about current friendships, how they shape behavior, and where new, supportive friends might be found.
benefits: The people a person spends time with can strengthen or weaken recovery, so reflecting on friendships helps steer toward supportive ones.

title: Mindful Breathing
involves: Choose one of three simple breathing exercises (noticing the breath, counting breaths, or belly breathing) and practice it for a few minutes.
benefits: Regular practice calms the body and mind and builds the ability to pause before reacting.

title: Introduction to Mindfulness
involves: Read what mindfulness is, why it helps, and a common misunderstanding about it, then reflect on moments of being on autopilot.
benefits: Mindfulness helps a person respond on purpose instead of reacting automatically, and can reduce stress and emotional overwhelm.

title: Motivation for Recovery
involves: Write down something important to protect, how alcohol harms it, and one small recovery action for this week, then keep that reason somewhere visible.
benefits: Keeping specific reasons in view steadies motivation, which naturally rises and falls, and links values to action.

title: Noticing Walk
involves: Take a 15 to 20 minute walk alone without a phone, focusing on sounds, smells, or sights, then jot down what was noticed.
benefits: Practicing present-moment awareness calms the mind and connects a person with their body and surroundings.

title: Special Occasions and Recovery
involves: Think of an upcoming holiday or special event, check off risk factors from a list, total the score, and read suggested steps for that level of risk.
benefits: Rating the risk of an event ahead of time shows how much extra planning and support it calls for.

title: Special Occasions and Drinking Associations
involves: For an upcoming event, write down the old drinking pattern, a new sober ritual, a support plan, an exit plan, and a backup plan if urges rise.
benefits: Planning before the event, when thinking is clear, helps keep meaningful occasions enjoyable without alcohol.

title: Daily Commitment Card
involves: Fill out a daily commitment card: one risk to avoid, one positive action, one person to contact, and a plan for urges today.
benefits: Narrowing the focus to today makes recovery feel manageable and builds long-term sobriety through small daily steps.

title: Overconfidence and Recovery
involves: Read how feeling fully in control after a stretch of progress can lead to dropping protective habits and testing limits, and a more balanced way of thinking about it.
benefits: Pairing confidence with ongoing caution helps a person keep the routines that are making their progress possible.

title: Physical Activity for Recovery Stability
involves: Build a menu of short, moderate, and social activity options, then schedule three activity sessions for the week.
benefits: Regular movement lowers stress, improves sleep and mood, can ease urges, and gives a ready alternative to drinking.

title: Planning Ahead for Challenging Events
involves: Before an upcoming risky event, fill out a plan covering triggers, goals, coping strategies, what to drink instead, support people, arrival and leaving times, and signs it is time to go.
benefits: Planning ahead, while thinking is clear, increases control and lowers risk once at the event.

title: Progressive Muscle Relaxation
involves: Follow a seven-minute guided video that tenses and then relaxes muscle groups one at a time.
benefits: Lowers physical tension and stress, which supports clearer thinking and better sleep.

title: Understanding Ambivalence About Abstinence
involves: Read why mixed feelings about quitting drinking are normal, how they show up, and ways to work through them, such as listing pros and cons and focusing on values.
benefits: Seeing mixed feelings as a normal part of change makes them easier to think through and helps a person set recovery goals for their own reasons.

title: Understanding Cravings
involves: Read about what cravings are, how they show up in the body, thoughts, and feelings, what sets them off, and simple ways to cope when one hits.
benefits: Knowing that cravings are normal, predictable, and short-lived makes them less alarming and easier to wait out.

title: Building Confidence in Recovery
involves: Read about self-efficacy, the belief that one can stay sober, and practical ways to build it, such as setting small goals, tracking wins, and positive self-talk.
benefits: Confidence grows with practice and helps a person handle challenges and bounce back from setbacks.

title: Understanding Slips in Recovery
involves: Read the difference between a lapse and a relapse, why lapses happen, and healthy ways to respond after one.
benefits: Treating a slip as a learning moment rather than a failure helps a person get back on track quickly.

title: Physical Health and Recovery
involves: Read how sleep, nutrition, exercise, hydration, and regular medical care support recovery.
benefits: A rested, well-fed body has more energy and clearer thinking for handling stress and urges.

title: Pleasant Events and Celebration
involves: Read why enjoyable events can still carry a pull toward drinking and strategies for enjoying them sober, such as planning ahead and bringing support.
benefits: Helps a person enjoy good times fully while staying prepared for the pull of old associations.

title: Relationships
involves: Read how relationships can support or challenge recovery, signs that a relationship may be risky, and ways to set boundaries and seek supportive connections.
benefits: Helps a person build a network of relationships that strengthens their sobriety.

title: Challenging Situations and Recovery
involves: Read what makes a situation risky, why people end up in them, and how to handle them by planning ahead, bringing support, and having an exit plan.
benefits: Knowing personal risky situations ahead of time lets a person prepare instead of being caught off guard.

title: Routine and Recovery
involves: Read how a steady daily routine of sleep, meals, work, exercise, and enjoyable activities supports recovery, with tips for building one.
benefits: Structure reduces stress and boredom and makes it easier to steer clear of situations that lead to drinking.

title: Stress and Recovery
involves: Read how stress affects the body, mind, and recovery, and healthy ways to manage it, such as relaxation, exercise, and support.
benefits: Managing stress in healthy ways reduces urges and protects the ability to make thoughtful choices.

title: Support Seeking in Recovery
involves: Read why support matters in recovery, signs that more support could help, and ways to build and keep a support network.
benefits: Having people to turn to brings encouragement, accountability, and help with solving problems.

title: Emotions and Recovery
involves: Read how difficult emotions such as sadness, anxiety, and anger can increase the pull toward drinking, and strategies for managing them.
benefits: Recognizing emotional patterns lets a person anticipate hard moments and cope in healthy ways.

title: Reasons for Not Drinking
involves: List reasons for not drinking, negative consequences of drinking, and situations that could make abstinence hard, rate commitment, and copy the lists onto a pocket card.
benefits: Having personal reasons written down and close at hand makes them easy to recall when thoughts of drinking come up.

title: Recognizing Stress
involves: Check off stress symptoms from the past month, total them, and reflect on the main sources of stress and one healthy way to start managing it.
benefits: Becoming aware of stress is the first step toward managing it without alcohol.

title: Recovery Progress Checklist
involves: Check off recovery behaviors already in place, such as avoiding triggers or attending meetings, and reflect on which have been easy, which are hard, and what to try next.
benefits: Recognizing changes already made builds a sense of progress and points to what to work on next.

title: Recovery Planning Worksheet
involves: Fill in a table covering work, friendships, finances, education, exercise, leisure, and meetings: where things stand now, goals, steps, and timing.
benefits: Setting concrete goals across life areas helps a person build a lifestyle that supports long-term recovery.

title: Recreational Activities
involves: List past hobbies worth revisiting and new activities to try, such as classes, sports, art, or volunteering.
benefits: Finding enjoyable, alcohol-free activities replaces the role drinking played in relaxing and having fun.

title: Reducing Stress
involves: Sort current stressors into ones that can be changed and ones that cannot, then pick one action for a changeable stressor and one coping skill for the other.
benefits: Separating what can be changed from what must be tolerated makes stress easier to manage and lowers vulnerability to risky decisions.

title: Patterns Before Drinking: A Look Back
involves: Think back to the week before the last lapse and fill in a table of events, behavior patterns, thoughts, and feelings across areas such as work, personal life, and health.
benefits: Identifying the patterns that came before a lapse helps a person recognize and interrupt them next time.

title: Patterns Before Drinking: Comparing Over Time
involves: Fill in the look-back table for a recent slip and compare it with any earlier look-back.
benefits: Spotting patterns that repeat over time shows which warning signs to watch for and which strategies have worked.

title: Noticing Drift in Recovery: Reading and Self-Assessment
involves: Read how relapse often starts as a gradual drift away from protective habits, then rate four statements about recent changes in recovery routines.
benefits: Catching drift early, while course correction is still easy, is one of the most effective ways to prevent relapse.

title: Mooring Lines: Interrupting Drift in Recovery
involves: List four or five specific behaviors that support recovery (the 'mooring lines') and triggers being avoided, then check them off on several different days.
benefits: Tracking these behaviors over time shows when recovery routines start to slip, so a person can act early.

title: Recovery Re-Engagement Plan
involves: Look at four areas of routine (schedule, support, stress management, sleep and health), choose a specific action to strengthen each, and set deadlines within 24 to 48 hours.
benefits: Taking quick, concrete action restores structure, and motivation often follows action rather than coming first.

title: Repairing Relationships
involves: Reflect on people who were hurt during drinking, how to make amends, whom to forgive, and what resentments to let go of.
benefits: Acknowledging past hurt can ease conflict in important relationships and helps a person begin to forgive themselves.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Restaurants
involves: Answer five questions about thoughts and urges that come up at restaurants, small decisions that raise risk, warning signs, and ways to prepare.
benefits: Thinking ahead helps a person dine out with confidence and stop risky choices before they build.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Challenging Places
involves: Answer five quick questions before going somewhere risky: why go, how honest the risk assessment is, what happened in the past, and whether it supports recovery.
benefits: Pausing to ask these questions helps a person catch a risky choice before acting on it.

title: The Importance of Scheduling
involves: Read why writing down a daily schedule supports recovery and how to get started, even for people who are not naturally organized.
benefits: A written plan, made while thinking is clear, makes it easier to follow through on recovery goals when urges push the other way.

title: Scheduling Worksheet
involves: Plan today or tomorrow hour by hour, including sleep, meals, work, exercise, recovery activities, and breaks, with space for notes and reminders.
benefits: Structured days leave fewer risky gaps and help a person balance responsibilities with self-care.

title: Alcohol Scripts in Nighttime Settings
involves: Journal on five prompts about what going out at night means, thoughts about drinking that come up, feelings about going out sober, and new beliefs that support not drinking.
benefits: Examining automatic links between nightlife and drinking makes it possible to enjoy evenings out in new ways.

title: Alcohol Scripts About the Weekend
involves: Journal on five prompts about expectations for weekends, thoughts about drinking as the weekend approaches, what drinking has given and taken away, and what a good weekend without alcohol would look like.
benefits: Questioning the link between weekends and drinking helps a person plan weekends that give real rest and enjoyment.

title: Alcohol Scripts in the Workplace
involves: Pick a high-risk work situation, identify the automatic thought and the need underneath it, challenge the thought, write a new one, and choose a replacement action.
benefits: Interrupting the loop from work stress to drinking gives healthier ways to unwind and handle work events.

title: Covering the Basics: Sleep, Food, and Rest
involves: Go through a checklist of basic self-care habits (sleep, meals, hydration, movement, rest, and more), then turn one unchecked item into today's goal.
benefits: Steady sleep, food, and rest reduce emotional reactivity and urges, which makes self-care a form of risk management.

title: Self-Talk
involves: Read how what people tell themselves about urges can make them stronger or weaker, then practice spotting an upsetting thought about an urge and challenging it.
benefits: Constructive self-talk makes urges feel more manageable and helps them pass without drinking.

title: Smart, Not Strong
involves: List situations where willpower is being relied on, write a smarter change to routine or surroundings for each, and try one change today.
benefits: Planning, structure, and support are more reliable than willpower, especially when stressed or tired.

title: Spirituality and Meaning
involves: Write a short paragraph for each of three prompts: what gives life meaning, what kind of person to be in recovery, and one daily action that reflects it.
benefits: Keeping meaning and values in view can give recovery a sense of purpose and make everyday choices feel more worthwhile.

title: Staying Busy with Purpose
involves: Journal on five prompts about unstructured time, what is really needed during it, and one small, realistic way to add structure to a vulnerable part of the day.
benefits: Meaningful structure reduces the boredom and rumination that can raise urges, and mood often improves once activity begins.

title: Taking Care of Yourself
involves: Answer eight questions about health and grooming, such as doctor and dentist visits, diet, exercise, and appearance, and write down the first self-care step to take.
benefits: Caring for health and appearance rebuilds self-respect and strengthens recovery.

title: Thought-Stopping
involves: Learn four ways to interrupt thoughts about drinking (picturing a switch, snapping a rubber band, slow deep breaths, and calling someone) and try the ones that work best.
benefits: Stopping a thought early keeps it from growing into a craving, and the skill gets stronger with practice.

title: Thought-Stopping Continued
involves: Learn five more ways to interrupt thoughts about drinking: a 'stop' command, picturing a stop sign, quick physical movement, writing the thought down, and switching to a healthy activity.
benefits: Having several tools ready increases the chance of stopping a thought before it becomes a craving.

title: Take Three Conscious Breaths
involves: Sit comfortably, close the eyes, and take three slow, deep breaths while noticing and letting go of tension; it takes about a minute.
benefits: A quick pause that calms the nervous system and can be used anywhere during stress or overwhelm.

title: Tracking Progress
involves: Mark each alcohol-free day on a calendar with a chosen symbol and review progress regularly with a counselor, sponsor, or friend.
benefits: Seeing the days add up gives a sense of pride and breaks a long recovery into manageable steps.

title: Tracking Triggers, Thoughts, and Behaviors
involves: Fill in a table for urges as they come up: what set them off, thoughts and feelings, what was done, and the positive and negative results.
benefits: Reviewing these patterns helps a person make healthier choices in similar situations.

title: Trigger Mapping
involves: For a recent place where urges came up, map the situation, trigger type, thoughts, feelings, urge level, what was done, which coping steps helped, and three things to do differently.
benefits: Breaking down one real situation reveals patterns and helps prepare effective coping for next time.

title: Trigger-Thought-Craving-Use
involves: Read how a trigger leads to a thought, the thought to a craving, and the craving to drinking, and why stopping the thought early matters.
benefits: Understanding this chain helps a person step in early, before a craving takes hold.

title: Understanding and Identifying Triggers
involves: Read an example of how everyday cues can set off cravings, then reflect on personal triggers, upcoming ones, and ways to avoid or cope with them.
benefits: Knowing personal triggers makes it possible to limit exposure and plan different responses.

title: Urge Surfing
involves: Learn a few simple steps for riding out an urge like a wave: acknowledge it, notice thoughts and feelings without fighting them, and remind oneself that it will pass.
benefits: Riding out an urge instead of acting on it shows that urges pass on their own, which makes them easier to handle over time.

title: Urge Surfing Practice
involves: During an urge, follow a short script (name it, notice it in the body, breathe, remind oneself it will pass) for a few minutes, then record the trigger, peak intensity, and how long it took to ease.
benefits: Each time an urge passes without drinking it loses strength, and tracking shows how quickly urges fade.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Weekend Plans
involves: Answer three short questions about plans for the coming weekend and whether having no plans could drift toward a risky situation.
benefits: Thinking ahead interrupts small choices that can lead toward drinking while they are still easy to change.

title: Reflecting on Decisions: Work
involves: Answer five questions about work situations that raise stress or urges, work habits that add risk, warning signs, and changes to work routines that support recovery.
benefits: Catching work-related risks early helps a person cope during and after work without drinking.
